extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers (particularly biomedical scientists), university faculty, members of hiring and grant committees, and readers interested in science publishing reform
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and norms for evaluating scientific work, publication venues, and peer-review practices in academic (especially biomedical) research; includes guidance for authors, editors, and hiring/grant committees on how to judge research quality and how publication incentives distort behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not evaluate researchers by journal impact factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Career decisions – be it an application for a job or a grant – tend to be based on the impact factors of the journals researchers publish in, rather than on the quality of the science they do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committees should never look at the journal in which a paper appeared when evaluating someone, and should speak up when anyone else does it. If evaluators judge people solely by manuscript contents, the incentive to target “luxury journals” will diminish and researchers will stop treating journal venue as the ticket to success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject 'significance' as a gatekeeping criterion for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Many top journals (and even some new journals) reject papers because they do not meet reviewers’ and editors’ standards of "significance" — a subjective judgment about how important or ‘sexy’ a work is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer journals that do not consider 'significance' (e.g., PLOS ONE, BMC) or change systems so significance is not used to gatekeep publication; this reduces perverse incentives to do extra experiments solely to make work more appealing to editors/reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits and problems of pre-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review isn't devoid of problems: relying on a few reviewers (and editors) to decide how significant a work is at the time is flawed and can misjudge or suppress good work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider alternative models such as dispensing entirely with journals or moving toward post-publication review where a broader community assesses significance over time, rather than a small set of pre-publication gatekeepers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use open-access and alternative publishing venues to break perverse incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: There are now plenty of alternatives (eLife, PLOS, BioMed Central and many others) that attack pathologies in science publishing, offering options beyond the big subscription 'luxury' publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should consider sending their best work to these alternatives (or to journals that do not use signficance as a publication filter) to reduce the allure and power of high-impact subscription journals and help change community norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt committee-level behavioral change as an effective lever
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical starting point for reform is on hiring and grant committees: changing how committees evaluate candidates can influence broader community behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee members should commit to not using journal venue as an evaluation proxy, actively resist others who do, and judge applicants by the contents of manuscripts — this will slowly shift expectations and reduce pressure on authors to pursue luxury journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid altering research priorities to chase perceived journal 'sexiness'
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers often spend months doing additional, sometimes pointless experiments to make their work ‘sexier’ to editors and reviewers at high-profile journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and advisers should resist reshaping or expanding projects solely to satisfy perceived editorial tastes; judging work on its intrinsic quality (not added 'sexiness') will reduce wasted effort and perverse experiment-driven behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that reputation and celebrity can substitute for venue but is not scalable
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly famous scientists (e.g., Nobel laureates) and their labs can attract attention regardless of venue, so their students/postdocs may not need a Nature/Science/Cell paper to be taken seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on reputation is an unfair and non-generalizable advantage; systemic reform must focus on community evaluation practices (not only individual boycotts by elite scientists) to make lasting change.
